_readme: THE ALARM-CHAIN LEDGER — the other half of tooling/monitor-register.json.
monitor-register.json answers 'does every hostname have a monitor'. This answers the question
nobody was asking: 'and if that monitor goes red, does a human find out'. They are different
questions and the second one had a NO in it for nine days.
WHY IT EXISTS. GlitchTip monitor 6 ('Laptop daily backup') was created with project_id = NULL.
The notification path is a single join — AlertRecipient.filter(alert__project__monitor__id=N,
alert__uptime=True), apps/uptime/tasks.py — so a monitor belonging to no project belongs to no
project's alert rule, and the recipient set comes back EMPTY. It went Down 13 times of 41 checks
and told nobody. Nothing was broken: the checks ran on schedule, the transitions were recorded,
the dashboard drew them red, the alert rule existed and was enabled. Every surface a person looks
at was healthy. The missing thing was a foreign key, and a foreign key has no dashboard.
🔴 chainsObserved IS THE POINT, AND IT IS NOT CONFIG. The obvious guard is 'assert every monitor
has a project', and verify-alarm-chains.mjs limb A is exactly that. But a config-shaped check
answers a config-shaped question, and it would have gone green the moment the foreign key was set
— which is the same half-state, one step later. So a chain is not complete here until somebody has
forced a real state change and watched a message land. Each entry must name evidence that outlives
the session that wrote it: a delivery record id, not the word 'verified'.
⚠️ Keys are PROJECT SLUGS, not project names. The alert rule hangs off the project, so the project
is the unit a chain is proven for — proving `ops` proves every monitor filed under `ops`. An early
draft of the guard keyed the API path by project NAME, which is identical to the slug for both of
today's projects and 404s for the first one that is not. It found that itself, during --self-test,
on a throwaway project called 'TEMP alarm-chain selftest'.
_expectedMonitorsWhy: 🔴 KEYED BY `id`, NEVER BY `name` — 2026-09-03, after a 46-hour production freeze.
This list used to be `expectedMonitorNames`. Moving GlitchTip from the Oracle box to the
Hostinger box renamed one monitor (`Oracle box backup chain` -> `GlitchTip backup chain
(Box B)`) because the NAME said which machine it was on. The rename was correct; the
declaration went stale; verify-alarm-chains reported COVERAGE LOST; Ops watch went red;
and the three register duties reading its run history aged out of a 36h window, freezing
EVERY MERGE AND BOTH DEPLOYS for ~46h.
A GlitchTip monitor `id` is a database primary key: it survives renames, project changes
and host moves, and changes only on delete-and-recreate — which is precisely the event
this canary SHOULD fail on. `name` here is a human label. It is printed on failure and
on drift, and it is NEVER asserted; a rename reports and does not redden.
⛔ DO NOT reintroduce a name comparison, and do not put a box name in a monitor name.
The ability to move a box without freezing deployments is the property this buys, and
with live users that property is the difference between a migration and an outage.
📌 AND THE LIST IS COMPLETE AS OF 2026-09-03, WHICH IT WAS NOT THE DAY BEFORE. Monitors 17
(`Supabase auth chain`), 18 (`Studio Access gate`) and 19 (`Supabase backup chain`) were created
live on 2026-09-02, the day of the Box B move, and appeared in NEITHER this file nor
tooling/monitor-register.json: twelve monitors live, nine declared. A canary that names nine of
twelve cannot notice the other three being deleted — so the gap was in the guard itself, not only
in the prose, and it opened on the same day and in the same move as the rename above. All twelve
are now listed.
⚠️ AND ALL THREE ARE DECLARED HERE AND NOWHERE ELSE, ON PURPOSE. 19 is a Heartbeat — no url, so
there is no hostname to file it under, the position monitors 6 and 16 have held since they were
made. 17 and 18 DO have hostnames, and are still not rows in tooling/monitor-register.json: that
file derives its rows from what THIS REPO deploys, and its rows are also [14]O-2's unauthenticated
probe set — auth-api.nikatru.com (api-auth before [ADR 080]) has no surface that probe can call healthy, measured. The full
reasoning is in that file under `_notInThisRegister`; a first attempt on 2026-09-03 made them rows
and had to be reverted. So THIS list is the only place a delete of any of the three fails a guard,
which is exactly what an id-keyed canary is for.
📌 AND IT WENT INCOMPLETE AGAIN ON 2026-09-05, WHICH IS WHY 'complete as of' CARRIES A DATE RATHER
THAN A TICK. Phase 3a created two more heartbeats on the same instance — 22 `Cloudflare D1/KV backup
pull` and 23 `Box B restic` — and for a few hours this list named twelve of fourteen. Both are now
listed. ⚠️ NOTE THE FAILURE MODE THIS FILE CANNOT CATCH BY ITSELF: limb D fails when a LISTED id is
absent from the live instance, and says nothing about a LIVE id that is absent from this list. That
asymmetry is deliberate — a canary that reddened on every newly created monitor would be red for the
minutes between creating one and declaring it, and people turn that kind of guard off — but it means
completeness here is maintained by whoever creates a monitor, not enforced. Both new ids also carry a
duty row in tooling/ops/register.json (`duty.cloudflare-backup-pull`, `duty.restic-snapshot`) whose
`recordQuery` reads the monitor by id on every CI run, so a delete of either now fails TWO guards.
⛔ 23's NAME CARRIES A BOX NAME, WHICH THIS SECTION'S OWN RULE FORBIDS. It is recorded and not
renamed: the id is the identity, a rename here is reported and never failed, and the register row
carries the same note. The rule is for the NEXT monitor somebody creates.
📌 AND FOUR MORE ON 2026-09-06 — 24 `Supabase dump`, 25 `Supabase Drive sync`, 26 `Supabase
second-copy sync`, 27 `Supabase disk alert`. They are the auth box's four wrapped root crons,
created live on 2026-09-05 and beaten before their register rows were written. This is the
asymmetry named two paragraphs up doing exactly what it does, and the numbers are measured rather
than eyeballed: `verify-alarm-chains` reads TWENTY live monitors from the instance today and this
list named FOURTEEN of them, and NOTHING went red, because limb D fails on a LISTED id that is
absent and is silent about a LIVE id that is unlisted. Completeness here is maintained by whoever
creates a monitor. All four also carry a duty row in tooling/ops/register.json
(duty.supabase-dump, duty.supabase-drive-sync, duty.supabase-second-copy, duty.supabase-disk-alert)
whose recordQuery reads the monitor by id on every CI run, so a delete of any of them now fails
TWO guards rather than none.
⚠️ 19 `Supabase backup chain` was ALREADY on this list and is deliberately NOT wrapped: it posts
its own beat only when the whole chain is healthy, so a wrapper beat asserting merely that the
script ran would be a weaker claim wearing the same monitor's clothes.
⬜ NOT CLOSED BY THIS ADDITION: no Down transition has been forced on any of 24-27, so none of
them appears in `chainsObserved` and none carries a `downTransitionDrill` anywhere. Being listed
here is a claim that the monitor still EXISTS, never that its alarm has been seen to arrive.
⬜ AND THE LIST IS STILL SHORT BY TWO, STATED HERE RATHER THAN QUIETLY CLOSED: ids 29 `Laptop
routine: ops check` and 30 `Laptop routine: CI watchdog` are live on the instance, are in no
`expectedMonitors` row, and have no duty row in tooling/ops/register.json either — so eighteen of
twenty are declared. They were not created by this change and adding an id whose duty nobody has
written would put this file ahead of the register it is supposed to agree with. It belongs to
whoever created them, and it is named so the next reader of 'complete as of' does not read a tick.
⏱ 2026-09-07, LATER THE SAME DAY — THE TWO COUNTS ABOVE MOVED. They are corrected HERE and the
sentences that carry them are left standing, because this file's own rule is that a frozen record
is superseded and never rewritten. `verify-alarm-chains` reads TWENTY live monitors and eighteen
of twenty are declared were both true when written this morning. RE-MEASURED THIS AFTERNOON:
`expectedMonitors` holds 20 rows (jq '.expectedMonitors | length' tooling/ops/alarm-chains.json)
and the live instance answers 22 monitors (GlitchTip list_monitors, org `nikatru`). IT IS TWENTY
OF TWENTY-TWO.
THE SHORTFALL DID NOT GROW, which is the only part a reader should act on. Both numbers moved by
exactly the same two ids — 31 `ntfy.nikatru.com` and 32 `vault.nikatru.com` — created by the
pager-monitors unit (ADR 067) and declared in the SAME change, so they were never undeclared. The
two live ids still in no `expectedMonitors` row and no duty row are still 29 `Laptop routine: ops
check` and 30 `Laptop routine: CI watchdog`, exactly the two the paragraph above names, and they
still belong to whoever created them. This correction exists because the paragraph above asks for
it in its own closing words: the list is named so the next reader of 'complete as of' does not
read a tick, and a count that has gone stale reads as a tick.
✅ 2026-09-09 — THE SHORTFALL THIS FILE HAS NAMED TWICE IS CLOSED, AND ONE NEW MONITOR IS DECLARED
IN THE SAME CHANGE THAT CREATED IT. The two paragraphs above say, twice, that 29 `Laptop routine:
ops check` and 30 `Laptop routine: CI watchdog` are live, undeclared here, carry no duty row, and
"belong to whoever created them". Nobody claimed them, and a monitor nothing declares is a monitor
whose DELETION nothing notices — which is not hypothetical here: three laptop routines vanished
unnoticed on 2026-09-08 and were rebuilt from scratch. That is the same event, one layer down.
Declared now: 29, 30, and 33 `Laptop routine: pipeline driver`, created 2026-09-09 for the third
routine, which had no absence alarm at all. Its shape is the one recorded as a recommendation and
not invented here: Heartbeat, project `ops`, interval 86400 s, confirmationThreshold 2. The
threshold is load-bearing rather than decorative — GlitchTip refuses any interval above 86400 s
(HTTP 422, `Input should be less than or equal to 86400`, the same wall duty.restic-snapshot
records hitting on 2026-09-05), and 86400 is EXACTLY the routine’s daily cadence, so a threshold
of 1 would take it Down on a few minutes of ordinary drift. A monitor that cries wolf daily gets
muted, which is the same outcome as no monitor, reached more slowly. Threshold 2 alarms after
roughly two missed days instead.
⚠️ THE ASYMMETRY NAMED ABOVE IS UNCHANGED AND IS WHY THIS PARAGRAPH EXISTS. Limb D fails on a
LISTED id that is absent from the live instance and stays silent about a LIVE id that is unlisted,
so completeness here is still MAINTAINED by whoever creates a monitor and is not ENFORCED. Measured
2026-09-09: the live instance answered 22 monitors before this change and this list named 20 of
them; creating 33 made it 23, and this list now names 23 of 23. That number is a measurement on a
date, not a tick — the two corrections above exist because a stale count reads as a tick.
🔴 AND THE DETECTION WAS PROVEN BY MUTATION, not by a green run. `verify-alarm-chains.mjs` was run
green first (exit 0, 23 of 23), then one of the three new ids was pointed at a monitor that does
not exist and the same script exited 1 naming it COVERAGE LOST; the file was restored with its
sha256 re-checked. A canary that has never been shown to fire is a claim, not a canary.

⏱ theDateMovedOn2026-09-07AndNOTHINGBELO: `date` is what verify-alarm-chains.mjs prints as 'delivery observed', so it points at the MOST
RECENT observation. Every field below — `monitor`, `how`, `evidence`, and both 🔴 blocks — is the
2026-08-05 record kept VERBATIM, because a frozen record is superseded, never rewritten ([ADR 053]
rule 2). The newer observation is `⏱ reObserved2026-09-07` immediately below, and it is stronger
in the two ways that matter: it ran against a REAL monitor rather than a throwaway, and it
exercised the ntfy hop on a real Down transition rather than the mail hop alone.

⏱ reObserved2026-09-07.monitor: vault.nikatru.com — monitor id 32, a REAL monitor in project `ops`, not a throwaway
⏱ reObserved2026-09-07.how: A full-replace PUT moved the monitor's `url` to https://vault.nikatru.com/alive-forced-down-drill-2026-09-07 (404) at 06:36:33Z and the whole object was diffed before and after — `url` was the only field that moved, so `project`, `confirmationThreshold` and `expectedBody` all survived the replace (TRAPS ci-10). First failing check 06:36:34Z with `isUp` STILL TRUE, second 06:37:06Z → `isUp` false. The PUT was reversed at 06:38:13Z, again diffed: the only fields differing from the pre-drill object were `isUp` and `lastChange`, which are runtime state. Vaultwarden itself was never touched and nothing on Box B was stopped.
⏱ reObserved2026-09-07.evidence: Read out of the `nikatru-page` ntfy topic cache with the `nikatru` account, not inferred from a 200: message EBnLsn48JilI at 06:37:09Z — title 'GlitchTip Uptime Alert', body 'vault.nikatru.com: The monitored site has gone down.' — THREE SECONDS after the transition; and message aC69SJL3P7TC at 06:38:17Z, '…is back up.', three seconds after recovery. Monitor 31 (ntfy.nikatru.com) produced its own 'back up' page at 06:34:53Z on creation, from the same rule.
⏱ reObserved2026-09-07.🔴 whatItDoesNOTProve: Nothing here narrows [pipeline E-9b]. The monitor, the alert evaluation, the webhook hop and ntfy itself are all on Box B. This drill proves the chain works while the box is alive, which is the failure that actually happens to a container — not the failure `_notObservable` names.
📌 twoStaleClaimsInTHISFILE, correctedByM: The 2026-08-05 block below says '⚠️ THE MESSAGE BODY IS RAW WEBHOOK JSON … it is not a defect, it
is the only shape that recipient type emits.' THAT IS NO LONGER WHAT LANDS. The webhook URL now
carries ntfy's own templating (`?tpl=yes` with `title` and `message` Go templates), so the two
messages quoted above arrive with a real title line and a one-sentence body. The old paragraph is
left standing because it was true when written and because its warning — that somebody will want
to 'fix' the shape — is what led to the fix.
And the RECIPIENT IDS MOVED. The block below records webhook recipient id 3 on rule 2 and id 4 on
rule 1; measured 2026-09-07 they are id 6 and id 5. The webhook recipients were REPLACED when the
templated URL landed — which is expected for a URL change — while the EMAIL recipients kept their
original primary keys, id 2 on rule 2 and id 1 on rule 1, exactly as the block below predicts a
non-destructive PUT should. The email leg is the one that has to survive, and it did.

ops.how: Shrank the heartbeat window to 60s so the production fetch() saw no heartbeat inside it, then enqueued the production perform_checks task — the same task dispatch_checks enqueues. Real Down transition 08:56:20Z, real recovery 08:57:01Z after a real POST to the heartbeat endpoint. Interval restored to 43200s; endpoint_id never changed, so the laptop's heartbeat URL still works.
ops.evidence: Two Resend delivery records to support@nikatru.com, both status=delivered: 4133761a-4c83-48eb-88e0-7af79aa2e8cc ('GlitchTip: Laptop daily backup is down', 08:56:23Z) and d87ac960-78df-4dce-b56a-f9c44efd6df8 ('… is back up', 08:57:03Z)
🔴 aSecondRecipientLandedOn2026-09-05, an: The `ops` alert rule (id 2, `uptime: true`, quantity 1 / timespan 1) gained a WEBHOOK recipient,
id 3, pointing at the self-hosted ntfy on the topic `nikatru-page`. Every monitor filed under `ops`
— 6, 16, 19 and now 22 and 23 — therefore reaches a PHONE as well as a mailbox on a Down
transition. The email recipient (id 2) kept its original primary key through the PUT, which is the
strongest available evidence that the recipient list was ADDED TO rather than replaced: this file
exists because a notification path silently lost its recipients once already.
🔴 IT DOES NOT CLOSE `_notObservable` BELOW, AND READING IT AS A SECOND PROVIDER WOULD BE THE
WORST MISREADING OF THIS ENTRY. ntfy runs on the SAME BOX as GlitchTip, the alert evaluation and
the Resend hop. A box death silences the monitor, the evaluation, the mail and the push in one
instant. Two recipients on one machine is redundancy against a mail-delivery failure, which is not
⚠️ AND IT IS CIRCULAR FOR EXACTLY ONE ALARM: an alert about ntfy being down cannot be delivered by
ntfy. The email recipient is what covers that case, which is one more reason it was added to and
⚠️ THE MESSAGE BODY IS RAW WEBHOOK JSON. GlitchTip's `webhook` recipient type emits one fixed
payload shape with no title line, so what lands on the phone is the envelope verbatim. Legible
enough to act on, ugly enough that somebody will want to 'fix' it — it is not a defect, it is the
only shape that recipient type emits.
ops.ntfyRouteEvidence: 2026-09-05 — proven end to end, not wired: a synthetic event fired into the `ops` DSN at 13:18:39 arrived on the `nikatru-page` topic at 13:19:37, 58 seconds later. Read back out of the topic's cache, not inferred from a 200. The webhook recipient is id 3 on alert rule id 2; the pre-existing email recipient id 2 survived the PUT unchanged.

subscriptiontracker.monitor: a throwaway monitor, deleted after the run
🔴 issuePathWasDeadUntilToday: THE UPTIME CHAIN BELOW WAS PROVEN, AND THE ISSUE CHAIN WAS DEAD — in the project that receives
every app crash. Alert rule 1 had quantity=null and timespanMinutes=null. GlitchTip's alert task
rule was invisible to issue alerts while continuing to work perfectly for uptime — because uptime
notifications come from a different task that never reads those fields.
Measured, not inferred: `Notification.objects.count()` was **1** across the entire instance, and
that one was an `ops` event created minutes earlier the same day. In the whole life of this
GlitchTip, subscriptiontracker had never produced a single crash notification. SUBLY-2 — a real fatal in the live
web app, `NoSuchMethodError: Null check operator used on a null value`, six occurrences across
2026-07-28/29 — came and went with nobody told.
Fixed to quantity=1 / timespan=1 and proven before-and-after: a probe sent with the nulls in place
created NO notification; the same probe after the fix produced notification #2 and a delivered
email. Both probes resolved. Now enforced by limb E of verify-alarm-chains.mjs.
📌 A project can be fully green on the uptime limb and completely silent on crashes. Proving one
and calling it 'the alert chain' is the mistake this entry exists to stop.
subscriptiontracker.issuePathEvidence: Resend delivery record 4452ae42-20f3-44eb-a046-c9932ff1b035 to support@nikatru.com, status=delivered, 'Error in subscriptiontracker: AFTER-FIX PROBE…', 12:57:09Z — subscriptiontracker's first crash-notification email ever
subscriptiontracker.how: This project's chain had never been observed either — it was only ever assumed, because its monitors were configured the way monitor 6 merely looked. Created a throwaway GET monitor in the project against a URL that 404s, ran the production perform_checks task, deleted it. No real monitor was altered and no real site was taken down.
subscriptiontracker.evidence: Resend delivery record 56bde711-db92-48c6-9eae-a0bb21660d18 to support@nikatru.com, status=delivered, 'GlitchTip: TEMP alarm-chain proof (delete me) is down', 08:58:40Z

_notObservable: 🔴 WHAT THIS LEDGER STILL CANNOT PROVE, stated so it is not mistaken for coverage.
Every monitor above, the alert evaluation, and the Resend SMTP hop all run on ONE box —
including monitor id 1, which watches GlitchTip itself. If that box is down, the check that would
notice is down and the mail that would say so is down with it, and the result is indistinguishable
from perfect health. Proving the chain delivers WHILE THE BOX IS UP says nothing about the case
that matters most. That is [pipeline E-9b], it is owner-gated, and it is recorded as undecided in
tooling/monitor-register.json → observability.spof. Do not read a green run of
verify-alarm-chains.mjs as an answer to it.
⚠️ THIS PARAGRAPH SAID 'ONE ORACLE BOX' UNTIL 2026-09-03, and the correction is one word rather
than a change of state. The box became the Hostinger box (Box B) on 2026-09-02 — the same move
whose rename is the subject of _expectedMonitorsWhy above, and the same move that put monitors 17,
18 and 19 on the instance. It is still ONE box, so E-9b is exactly as open as it was; naming the
old text is how a reader can tell a correction from a resolution.
🔴 AND THERE IS A SECOND ALERTING PATH ON THAT BOX THIS LEDGER DOES NOT COVER AT ALL — recorded
2026-09-05 so 'absent from this file' cannot be mistaken for 'does not exist'. Beszel (the host-metrics
hub, `/opt/beszel`) carries SIX alerts of its own — disk > 80%, memory > 85%, system down 2 min, on each
of the two boxes — and they route straight to the same ntfy topic through shoutrrr, never touching
GlitchTip. So a box going down has two independent detectors and this file can only ever speak for one
of them. The Beszel route was proven with a REAL outage rather than a test button: `docker stop
beszel-agent` for 270 s produced ntfy message 1788617561 'Connection to box-b-hostinger is down' and
1788617681 '… is up' on restart.
⚠️ IT IS NOT A ROW HERE AND SHOULD NOT BECOME ONE. Every limb of verify-alarm-chains.mjs is a query
against the GlitchTip API — projects, alert rules, recipients, monitors — and Beszel has none of those.
A row for it would be a claim this script cannot re-check, which is the config-shaped coverage this
whole file was written against. What it IS: a second detector on the same box, which narrows nothing
about E-9b, because Beszel, its alerts and ntfy all die with that box too.
